prompt:
Extract a SysML v2 model from the document as a list of facts. Each fact has unit_id (the sentence it comes from), type and slots. Give only the slots that have a value, as a list of {slot, value} pairs; for composition give one 'parts' pair per part.

Types and slots:
  attribute(owner,name,value,unit) action(performer,label) state(owner,label) constraint(subject,expression) requirement(subject,text)
  composition(whole,parts) flow(source,target,payload) succession(before,after) transition(from,to,trigger) allocation(action,to)

Name each element by its full name as first introduced in the document.
RULES:
- Resolve every entity-valued slot using all the text you are given. If a sentence refers to an element by an alias, abbreviation, pronoun or shorter description, write the element's full name as first introduced. If a sentence says an element receives or uses an item and the text you are given states which element produces or sends that item, emit a flow from that producer to the receiver. If an element cannot be determined from the text you are given, use null; never guess.
- Never write placeholder words such as "any", "all", "some state" for an unstated element; use null.
- Do not merge differently named things unless the text says they are the same.
- Emit one action for EVERY behavior verb phrase, including passive voice (performer null), capability statements, displays, logs, generates and reports. label = the verbatim verb phrase with its object.
- Emit a requirement for every NORMATIVE statement (shall, must, should, will, is required to, needs to). Purpose, goal or benefit sentences are not requirements.
- Emit a state for every named mode or state; transitions use the state names, with from null when the prior state is not stated.
- Emit a succession only for an EXPLICIT temporal connective between two actions ("then", "after", "once", "before", "when ... is complete", "next", "finally"); before/after are the action labels. Never use succession for cause or data transfer.
- Resolve a pronoun or "this/these" performer to the element named in the preceding sentence and write that element's name; if it cannot be resolved, use null. Never output a pronoun as a slot value.
- Drop determiners and quantifiers from element names ("Each Soil Moisture Probe" -> "Soil Moisture Probe", "the system" -> "system").
- allocation.to must be a component or actor, never a mode or state.
- Emit a constraint for every threshold, limit, period or deadline stated with a number; expression = the verbatim phrase.
- Emit a flow for every sentence in which an element sends, transmits, reports, displays, commands or delivers an item (target null if the receiver is not named).
 Also list under "entities" every system element, actor or item named in the document units, with its full name and any alias the text explicitly declares for it (e.g. 'hereafter X', 'known as X', 'called X'); aliases [] if none. Return JSON {"entities": [...], "facts": [...]}.

Memory from EARLIER parts of the document (do not extract facts from it; use it only to resolve names, aliases and who produces an item):
Context: FAA NextGen aims to increase National Airspace System (NAS) capacity/efficiency. En route ops suffer in adverse weather (convection, winds, turbulence, snow/ice, low visibility/ceilings; ~70% of US delays); a 2015 NASA survey found weather delays the costliest en route problem. System of interest: NASA Airspace Technology Demonstrations 3 (ATD-3), integrated ground- and aircraft-based technologies/decision aids that continuously search for more efficient weather-avoidance routes, respond rapidly to weather changes and Traffic Management Initiatives (TMIs), and enable continued en route/arrival metering in weather. Subset: NASA Dynamic Weather Routes (DWR), cruise phase, using existing weather/airspace/traffic data, improved navigation/surveillance/communication/digital networks and existing ATM automation to offset strategic flow management and forecast uncertainty; benefits: time, fuel, cost savings. Current system: TMIs divert/meter traffic when demand exceeds air traffic control (ATC) capacity, overly conservatively. FAA traffic managers designate Flow Constrained Areas (FCA) and implement Severe Weather Avoidance Plans (SWAP), aka Playbook routes, identified 2-8 h ahead; static, conservative, prioritizing weather avoidance, then controller workload, then route efficiency. Airline flight dispatchers file flight plans at least 45 min before push-back (typically 1-2 h before take-off) using forecasts, and file revised routes per applicable SWAP routes. Collaborative Trajectory Options Program (CTOP) lets operators file multiple routes on one flight plan per departure delay and preferences; still strategic, no post-departure improvement. Air traffic controllers, dispatchers and pilots can manually identify/request route amendments but workload is very high and in-flight changes need heavy coordination. Flight crews use flight management systems and on-board weather radar but cannot see convection beyond radar range nor congestion/traffic conflicts. Gaps: no automation notifies when constraints end or identifies time/fuel-saving corrections to stale routes; aircraft stay on circuitous routes, incurring delay and fuel. No modes or normative requirements stated yet.

Document units:
U0040: They often must consult either the controller or airline dispatch about alternate trajectories that will avoid large areas of adverse weather and flow restrictions, and must coordinate with the controller to ensure an alternate trajectory will not conflict with another aircraft.
U0041: Therefore, automation tools for controllers, dispatchers, and/or flight crews that can continuously monitor real-time and short-term weather forecasts, and dynamically find workable opportunities for time- and fuel-saving corrections to weather avoidance routes, have the potential to significantly improve the efficiency in both en route and terminal transition airspace. 4 DYNAMIC WEATHER ROUTES (DWR) SYSTEM DESCRIPTION Over the past several years, NASA has developed and tested a ground-based concept called Dynamic Weather Routes (DWR) to automatically identify opportunities for more efficient trajectories around convective constraints [2][3][10].
U0042: DWR is trajectory-based concept that continuously and automatically analyzes in-flight aircraft within en route airspace to find simple amendments to flight plan routes that can save significant flying time, while accounting for convective weather, traffic conflicts, airspace sector congestion, special use airspace, and FAA routing restrictions.
U0043: DWR then alerts the user to proposed route corrections and allows them to view and modify the route prior to requesting or issuing a new route clearance.
U0044: Additionally, the DWR user interface provides strong warnings if a user modifies a DWR route such that its trial trajectory conflicts with forecast weather or traffic.
U0045: Because there are various methods and degrees to which DWR could be implemented in FAA automation systems, the term “automation” as used in this paper is intended to be generic unless specified otherwise.
U0046: DWR is an extension of the Direct-To tool developed and tested at NASA from 1998 through 2001 [4], and as a result the Direct-To functionality of identifying conflict free, operationally acceptable, direct route clearances is an integral part of DWR.
U0047: Any Direct-To route that meets the minimum wind- corrected, time-savings criteria (user-definable) will appear as a DWR route correction advisory regardless of the presence of convective weather.
U0048: Although DWR is designed to address weather related inefficiencies, its underlying logic of identifying and avoiding constraints defined by polygons would enable it to be applied to non-weather related obstacles.
U0049: Doing so could result in substantial benefits in the form of fuel, emissions and controller/pilot workload savings.
